# Illinois — Commercial UAS Regulatory Summary

**Prepared for:** AEC (surveying, mapping, construction, inspection) UAS program management
**Research date:** August 1, 2026 | **Version:** 2.1 (Phase 2 — subjective-scope audit complete August 2, 2026)
**Model / checkpoint:** Claude Sonnet 5 (research and drafting)
**Interpretation scope:** Agent Instructions v6 (August 2, 2026)
**Scope note:** Federal FAA Part 107 is the baseline for all commercial sUAS operations nationwide and is not restated here. Per current research-phase scope (Agent Instructions v6, Amendment 2), this summary covers Illinois **state and state-agency** UAS authorities only — local ordinances are largely, but not entirely, foreclosed: 620 ILCS 5/42.1 makes UAS regulation an exclusive state power and bars local ordinances, but (i) it carves out any municipality of more than 1,000,000 inhabitants (currently only Chicago, which has its own drone ordinance, not researched here), and (ii) a separate subsection preserves any local government's right to adopt "reasonable rules" governing UAS use of airspace above its own parks/recreation/conservation land. Full citations and metadata are in `IL_UAS_Source_Register.csv`.

> **Process note (Agent Instructions Amendment 5, August 2, 2026):** Phase 2 practical interpretation and the completed-state subjective-scope audit are complete for the authorities presented below. The four labeled perspectives normally use one to three sentences, but may run longer when relevant and needed; they are operational and risk-management interpretations of the verified research packet, do not add legal requirements, and are not legal advice.

Each authority below is presented as an **Objective Summary** (binding text/citation, no interpretation) followed by **Practical Interpretation** from four labeled perspectives: AEC Industry UAS Expert, Agency Practitioner, UAS Procurement Expert, and AEC Industry Legal Counsel. Practical interpretation is not legal advice.

---

## 1. State UAS Regulatory Overview

Illinois regulates UAS primarily through a small set of targeted statutes rather than one omnibus drone act. The Freedom from Drone Surveillance Act (725 ILCS 167) restricts *law enforcement* drone use, not private commercial operation, but is the state's most heavily litigated and amended UAS statute. Separately, 620 ILCS 5/42.1 makes UAS regulation an exclusive state function and preempts local ordinances statewide — except for Chicago (population over 1,000,000) and a narrower carve-out letting any local government adopt "reasonable rules" for UAS use over its own park/recreation/conservation land. The Wildlife Code (520 ILCS 5/2.33(i)) bars using a drone to harass wildlife, with a notable exception for utility/mobile-service infrastructure inspection. State-facility-specific rules exist for the Capitol Complex (which expressly recognizes construction-documentation flights as an approvable use) and for IDNR-administered state parks and land (which require site-specific landing authorization under a rule that does not, on its face, name drones). IDOT's Division of Aeronautics runs an active UAS program for consultants/contractors and, as of March 2026, has imposed an indefinite ban on FASC-listed foreign-manufactured UAS (including DJI and Autel) on any IDOT project with a federal-funding nexus — a currently disruptive, fast-moving policy for AEC firms doing IDOT-funded inspection and mapping work. Two additional bills — one addressing government-agency UAS procurement/country-of-origin restrictions and sensitive-site geofencing, another creating private-operator-facing critical-infrastructure and correctional-facility no-fly offenses — remain pending in the General Assembly and are not yet law.

## 2. Statewide UAS Laws and Regulations

### Freedom from Drone Surveillance Act — 725 ILCS 167
*Binding law | Current, originally P.A. 98-569 (2014), substantially amended by P.A. 103-101 (eff. 6-16-23)*

**Objective Summary:** Prohibits a "law enforcement agency" from using a drone to gather information except under 10 enumerated exceptions in Section 15 (e.g., a Section 108-3 search warrant; exigent circumstances/imminent harm; disaster or public-health emergency; missing-person search and rescue; crime-scene/traffic-crash photography; infrastructure inspection at a local government's request; public-relations demonstration with no data collection; PSAP-dispatched emergency response; and monitoring a "routed event" or "special event" with advance public notice). Sections 17–18 separately bar onboard facial recognition and equipping a law-enforcement drone with any weapon. Section 20 requires destruction of gathered information within 30 days (24 hours for event-monitoring use), Section 25 restricts disclosure, Section 30 creates a presumption of inadmissibility for information gathered in violation of the Act, Section 35 requires annual public reporting to the Illinois Criminal Justice Information Authority, and Section 45 gives the Attorney General pattern-and-practice investigation and injunctive authority, including a 6–12 month drone-use forfeiture remedy.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Design acquisition and data-handling workflows to minimize unnecessary capture of people and private activity. Confirm the source-supported consent or project-purpose basis before flight and carry that limitation through processing, access control, retention, and delivery.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Treat the cited authority as a documented compliance gate where applicable. Preserve the facts supporting any exception or consent theory, allocate client and operator responsibilities clearly, and seek state counsel when project facts approach ambiguous or penal language.
### Regulation of Unmanned Aircraft Systems — State Preemption of Local Ordinances — 620 ILCS 5/42.1
*Binding law | Current, text as amended by P.A. 103-925 (eff. 8-9-24)*

**Objective Summary:** Makes UAS regulation "an exclusive power and function of the State" to the extent state oversight doesn't conflict with federal law, and bars any unit of local government — including home-rule units — from enacting an ordinance or resolution regulating UAS; this does not apply to a municipality of more than 1,000,000 inhabitants (currently only Chicago). Subsection (b-5) separately preserves a local government's right to adopt "reasonable rules" for a private party's use of airspace above its own recreational/conservation property (parks, playgrounds, wildlife areas, etc.), provided those rules don't conflict with state agency rules or federal law. Subsection (d) authorizes IDOT to adopt UAS safety rules.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Plan environmental and mapping flights to avoid conduct that could be characterized as locating, pursuing, disturbing, or harassing wildlife. Coordinate mission timing and stand-off distances with the land manager when project work overlaps sensitive habitat or hunting activity.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Document the applicability analysis and any exception relied upon in the project file. Align the scope, client representations, and operator procedures with the verified authority, and seek state counsel if material facts fall outside its clear terms.
### Wildlife Code — Prohibition on Using Unmanned Aircraft to Take, Pursue, or Harass Wildlife — 520 ILCS 5/2.33(i)
*Binding law | Current, provision most recently reflected in P.A. 103-154 (eff. 6-30-23)*

**Objective Summary:** Makes it unlawful to take, pursue, or intentionally harass or disturb wild birds or mammals by use or aid of a vehicle, conveyance, or unmanned aircraft (as defined by the Illinois Aeronautics Act), except as federally permitted for waterfowl taking. The subsection exempts using an unmanned aircraft to inspect a public utility facility, tower, or structure, or a mobile-service facility, tower, or structure, by the utility or provider itself.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Plan environmental and mapping flights to avoid conduct that could be characterized as locating, pursuing, disturbing, or harassing wildlife. Coordinate mission timing and stand-off distances with the land manager when project work overlaps sensitive habitat or hunting activity.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Treat the cited authority as a documented compliance gate where applicable. Preserve the facts supporting any exception or consent theory, allocate client and operator responsibilities clearly, and seek state counsel when project facts approach ambiguous or penal language.
### Unmanned Aerial Systems Security Act — SB 2364 (proposed — not enacted)
*Proposed or pending authority | Introduced 2/6/2025; last action 2/7/2025 (referred to Assignments); no further action recorded*

**Objective Summary:** Would bar a government agency from purchasing, acquiring, or using a drone (or related services/equipment) produced by a manufacturer domiciled in, or reasonably believed to be owned/controlled by, a "country of concern," using a 3-tier drone classification and a reimbursement fund for agencies holding non-compliant equipment. Would also require IDOT to identify "sensitive location" coordinates and require flight-mapping-software providers to geofence them, making unauthorized sensitive-location overflight (or software facilitation of one) a Class A misdemeanor. As introduced, proposes a January 1, 2026 effective date, contingent on passage. **This bill has not passed either chamber of the General Assembly and is not current law.**

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Treat this record as a research flag, not an operator requirement. Do not change field procedures unless a current controlling source confirms the issue; route any project-specific uncertainty to the identified agency or counsel.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** No current state equipment restriction is established by this research result. Do not treat that absence as permanent; check current solicitation terms, client policies, and independently applicable federal restrictions before committing a fleet to the work.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Do not present this negative or unresolved research result as a legal conclusion. Preserve the research limitation, verify current authority for the specific project, and escalate only if the issue could materially affect scope, access, or liability.
### Drone Safety and Interference Prevention Act — SB 3930 / HB 5275 (proposed — not enacted)
*Proposed or pending authority | HB 5275 through House Judiciary-Criminal Committee and to Second Reading, then re-referred to Rules 4/17/2026 after a floor amendment; SB 3930 in Senate committee process, last action 3/27/2026*

**Objective Summary:** Would create three new offenses — unlawful imaging of an emergency-response activity, unlawful operation over a critical infrastructure facility, and unlawful operation over a correctional institution or facility — and would bar any private person or entity from equipping a drone with a firearm, weaponized laser, kinetic-impact projectile, chemical agent/irritant, or other lethal/non-lethal weapon. Provides for law-enforcement seizure and court-supervised forfeiture of a violating drone, with notice/hearing protections and civil immunity for good-faith enforcement. As introduced, proposes a January 1, 2027 effective date, contingent on passage. **Neither bill has passed a full chamber and neither is current law.**

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Track this authority before mobilization, but do not treat a proposal, repealed measure, or superseded source as a current operating rule. Base the flight plan on the verified law and agency policy then in force.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Separate current law from legislative or historical context in advice and contract documents. Recheck status at project kickoff and before mobilization, and avoid representing a proposal, vetoed measure, or superseded source as binding.
## 3. State Agency and Facility-Specific UAS Requirements

### Illinois Capitol Complex — Operating Unmanned Aircraft on the Capitol Complex (71 Ill. Adm. Code 2005.65)
*Binding administrative regulation | Current, adopted 11-16-23*

**Objective Summary:** Closes the Capitol Complex (State-owned/occupied buildings, grounds, parking lots, and airspace within defined Springfield boundaries) to launching, landing, or operating a UAS, subject to five exceptions (emergency response; health/safety-emergency support; national defense; care-and-custody activities with prior Director approval; and construction-site documentation flights authorized by the Office of the Architect of the Capitol with advance notice to the Director). Absent an exception, a person may seek advance written approval from the Director of the Secretary of State's Department of Police, who evaluates public-safety, property-damage, interference, and scheduling-conflict factors and may impose time/place/manner conditions. All FAA requirements apply independently.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Add this authority to the state-specific preflight checklist and confirm its applicability to the project site, mission purpose, and client. Document the operational decision and any source-supported exception before dispatch.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Contact the facility authority identified by Illinois Secretary of State, Department of Police before mobilization; do not treat client access or a general work order as the required UAS approval. Ask for the current written-authorization route, security review, notice period, required crew and aircraft information, and on-site coordination conditions, and retain the issued authorization.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Document the applicability analysis and any exception relied upon in the project file. Align the scope, client representations, and operator procedures with the verified authority, and seek state counsel if material facts fall outside its clear terms.
### Illinois Department of Natural Resources — State Park/Land Aircraft Landing Authorization (17 Ill. Adm. Code 110.160(i))
*Binding administrative regulation | Current*

**Objective Summary:** Makes it unlawful, except in emergencies, to land or attempt to land any aircraft on IDNR-owned, -leased, or -managed property (including State parks) without prior Department authorization for each landing or attempted landing. The provision's text uses the general term "aircraft," not a UAS-specific term; IDNR's own site-level practice treats this as applicable to drone launches/landings and requires site-by-site written permission (coordinated through the relevant Site Superintendent or IDNR's Office of Land Management) before any drone flight originating from or landing on IDNR land.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Build the issuing agency approval into pre-mobilization planning. Confirm the property boundary, current submission materials, operating dates, and issued conditions before dispatch, and leave schedule contingency because the captured source does not guarantee processing time.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Start with the site manager or permitting office for Illinois Department of Natural Resources (IDNR) before scheduling fieldwork, because property-specific conditions may control the route and timing. Request the current form, lead time, fee, insurance and FAA-document checklist, and site restrictions, then keep the signed approval and conditions in the mission file.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Make the required approval and compliance with its conditions a documented mobilization gate. Allocate responsibility for applications and schedule impacts in the contract, and obtain counsel if the project's facts do not fit the stated authorization pathway.
### Illinois Department of Transportation, Division of Aeronautics — UAS Program and Foreign-Made-UAS Restriction
*Official agency policy | Current; restriction memo dated March 18, 2026, in place indefinitely*

**Objective Summary:** IDOT's Division of Aeronautics administers an active UAS program and requires contractors/consultants operating UAS in support of an IDOT project to first contact the Division to confirm they may legally operate. As of March 18, 2026, IDOT — implementing the federal American Security Drone Act of 2023 and OMB Memo M-26-02 — prohibits use of Federal Acquisition Security Council (FASC)-prohibited-manufacturer UAS (named examples include DJI and Autel) on any IDOT project or activity with a federal-funding nexus, including phase 1/2 work likely to draw federal funding later. This applies to IDOT-owned equipment and expressly to third-party contractor/consultant UAS. IDOT states it is coordinating with FHWA toward a resolution but has been given no timeline; the restriction is described as in place indefinitely.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Add this authority to the state-specific preflight checklist and confirm its applicability to the project site, mission purpose, and client. Document the operational decision and any source-supported exception before dispatch.
- **Agency Practitioner:** For work subject to this policy, contact the agency project manager and Illinois Department of Transportation (IDOT), Division of Aeronautics before fixing the mobilization date. Submit the proposed aircraft and payload configuration, operator credentials, flight purpose and location, insurance evidence, and any federal authorization the agency requests; retain the agency's confirmation and project-specific conditions.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** Require current vendor documentation for aircraft, critical components, installed software, ownership, origin, and support lifecycle before purchase. Compare the proposed configuration with the controlling authority and preserve the evidence supporting the acquisition decision.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Describe this source as guidance or policy, not a generally binding statute. Check whether the client or property owner incorporates it contractually, preserve the version relied upon, and escalate conflicts with controlling authority.
### Professional Licensing — Illinois Professional Land Surveyor Act of 1989 (225 ILCS 330/5)
*Binding general regulation | No UAS-specific board guidance located*

**Objective Summary:** Defines the "practice of land surveying" to include boundary, configuration, contour, and fixed-object determination — except as performed by photogrammetric methods by a person holding ASPRS (or substantially similar, Department-approved) certification, or where the required accuracy is below the National Society of Professional Surveyors Model Standards. No standalone IDFPR or Illinois Land Surveyors Licensing Board guidance specifically addressing UAS-derived photogrammetry, LiDAR, or mapping products was located.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Classify the intended UAS-derived deliverable before mobilization and place licensed-professional review where the verified authority requires it. Keep flight acquisition, analysis, and final professional deliverable responsibilities explicit in the project workflow.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Before relying on an unlicensed or exempt delivery path, give Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation (IDFPR) / Illinois Land Surveyors Licensing Board a written description of the proposed UAS-derived product, its stated accuracy, and whether it will establish or certify boundaries, elevations, or authoritative locations. Ask the board to confirm the applicable license, responsible-charge, certification, or exemption path and retain the response with the project quality plan; the research packet does not establish a UAS-specific turnaround time.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** Not applicable — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Describe this source as guidance or policy, not a generally binding statute. Check whether the client or property owner incorporates it contractually, preserve the version relied upon, and escalate conflicts with controlling authority.
### Executive Orders, AG Opinions, Court Decisions, and Procurement
*Categories reviewed — none dispositive located*

**Objective Summary:** No Illinois gubernatorial executive order specifically and solely addressing UAS regulation was located. No formal Illinois Attorney General opinion construing a UAS-specific statute was located; the Attorney General's office has published non-regulatory guidance to law enforcement agencies on drone usage under 725 ILCS 167 and holds pattern-and-practice investigation/injunctive authority under that Act's Section 45, but this is law-enforcement-directed agency guidance, not a formal opinion, and is not separately regulatory of private AEC operators. No Illinois appellate court decision directly construing 725 ILCS 167, 620 ILCS 5/42.1, or 520 ILCS 5/2.33(i) was located. No general statewide state-agency UAS procurement or approved-manufacturer statute currently in force was located beyond the IDOT-specific federal-nexus policy above and the not-yet-enacted SB 2364.

**Practical Interpretation**

- **AEC Industry UAS Expert:** Treat this record as a research flag, not an operator requirement. Do not change field procedures unless a current controlling source confirms the issue; route any project-specific uncertainty to the identified agency or counsel.
- **Agency Practitioner:** Not applicable — no agency process.
- **UAS Procurement Expert:** No current state equipment restriction is established by this research result. Do not treat that absence as permanent; check current solicitation terms, client policies, and independently applicable federal restrictions before committing a fleet to the work.
- **AEC Industry Legal Counsel:** Do not present this negative or unresolved research result as a legal conclusion. Preserve the research limitation, verify current authority for the specific project, and escalate only if the issue could materially affect scope, access, or liability.
## 4. Non-Regulatory Context

*The items below are drawn from news and secondary reporting, not primary legal authority. They are provided for situational awareness only and are not part of the verified source register.*

- **FAA imposes unprecedented drone restriction over Chicago amid immigration enforcement operation, NBC News, October 2, 2025.** The FAA, at DHS's request, imposed a temporary flight restriction covering a roughly 15-nautical-mile radius around O'Hare (up to 400 ft) for non-governmental drones, citing a "credible threat" of attacks on federal agents during an immigration-enforcement operation; the restriction was reported to run through approximately October 12, 2025, with waiver exceptions for specific governmental/commercial activity. This is directly relevant to any AEC UAS program with Chicago-area flight plans, since ordinary Part 107 operations can be abruptly grounded by a federally-imposed, non-statutory TFR with little advance notice. [Source](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/chicago-airspace-restricted-threats-agents-faa-homeland-security-rcna235482)
- **Oak Brook Police Department launches Illinois' first fully autonomous drone-as-first-responder program, ABC7 Chicago, August 15, 2025.** Oak Brook (a Chicago suburb) began operating a Flock Safety autonomous drone dispatched from police headquarters to calls across its 8-square-mile jurisdiction, providing live video and license-plate data to a real-time crime center — reported as the first fully autonomous program of its kind in the state. This illustrates how Illinois law enforcement agencies are operationalizing the PSAP-dispatch and event-monitoring exceptions in 725 ILCS 167 (IL-001) in current practice. [Source](https://abc7chicago.com/post/oak-brook-police-department-launches-fully-autonomous-drone-first-responder-concerned-privacy-rights/17539659/)
- **Illinois bill would require registered sex offenders to disclose drone ownership to state police, DroneXL, February 25, 2026.** State Rep. Katie Stuart introduced HB 4332, which would add drone ownership (make and model) to the existing disclosure list under the Illinois Sex Offender Registration Act; the bill does not restrict drone operation or create a new surveillance program, only a registrant disclosure requirement. It had not been enacted as of this research date and is not yet reflected in the source register. [Source](https://dronexl.co/2026/02/25/illinois-bill-sex-offenders-register-drones/)
- **Drone pilot arrested for flying into restricted airspace during sold-out Illinois-Kansas football game, The News-Gazette (Champaign-Urbana), September 2024.** University of Illinois police, aided by SkySafe drone-detection technology, tracked a drone that entered Memorial Stadium's restricted airspace and hovered near a SWAT overwatch position to an operator on a nearby balcony within minutes; the operator was arrested and charged with reckless conduct. The incident illustrates active enforcement of stadium/event no-fly restrictions at major Illinois public-university venues. [Source](https://www.news-gazette.com/news/local/courts-police-fire/memorial-stadium-sees-only-one-arrest-during-sold-out-illinois-kansas-game/article_f6c545da-6ef5-11ef-8020-7bd26b92324f.html)

## 5. Unresolved Operational Questions

- **620 ILCS 5/42.1(b-5) local park/recreation-land rules:** Any Illinois park district, forest preserve district, or municipality could have adopted its own "reasonable rules" for UAS use over its own recreational/conservation land under this subsection; no statewide inventory of such local rules was compiled in this pass — confirm directly with the relevant local land-managing agency before assuming state preemption fully controls a specific site.
- **17 Ill. Adm. Code 110.160(i) "aircraft" scope:** This IDNR park-land rule does not use a UAS-specific term; its application to drones rests on IDNR site practice and general inference, not on rule text naming drones — confirm directly with IDNR's Office of Land Management before relying on this citation.
- **IDOT FASC-prohibited-manufacturer restriction:** Described by IDOT as in place "indefinitely" with no resolution timeline; AEC firms with pending or planned IDOT-funded UAS work should confirm current status and permitted airframes directly with the Division of Aeronautics before mobilizing equipment, as this is a fast-moving, currently unresolved policy.
- **SB 2364 and SB 3930/HB 5275 (pending legislation):** Neither the procurement/country-of-origin bill nor the critical-infrastructure/correctional-facility bill has been enacted; both should be monitored for advancement in the current or a future General Assembly session, since either would materially change the regulatory landscape for AEC UAS work in Illinois if passed.
- **225 ILCS 330/5 photogrammetric-methods exception:** Whether a specific UAS-derived deliverable falls inside or outside licensed land-surveying practice is fact-specific (accuracy achieved, operator certification) and was not resolved against current IDFPR/Board guidance in this pass.
- **Local ordinances (Chicago and elsewhere):** Chicago's own drone ordinance (available under the 620 ILCS 5/42.1(b) population exception) and any local 42.1(b-5) rules are out of scope for this Phase 1, state-level pass.

## 6. Confidence Summary

| Finding | Confidence |
|---|---|
| 725 ILCS 167 (Freedom from Drone Surveillance Act — law enforcement UAS use) | High — verified directly against the Illinois General Assembly's own codification |
| 620 ILCS 5/42.1 (state preemption, Chicago exception, and local-recreational-land carve-out) | High — verified directly against ILGA's own published document |
| 520 ILCS 5/2.33(i) (Wildlife Code drone-harassment prohibition and utility-inspection exception) | High — verified directly against ILGA's own published document |
| 71 Ill. Adm. Code 2005.65 (Capitol Complex UAS rule) | High — verified directly against a current codification mirror |
| 17 Ill. Adm. Code 110.160(i) (IDNR land aircraft-landing authorization) | Moderate — rule text confirmed, but its application to "drones" specifically rests on inference/site practice, not rule text |
| IDOT Division of Aeronautics UAS program and FASC-manufacturer restriction | High — verified directly against IDOT's own webpage and memo |
| SB 2364 (Unmanned Aerial Systems Security Act) | High confidence that it is **not current law**, verified against ILGA's own bill-status page |
| SB 3930 / HB 5275 (Drone Safety and Interference Prevention Act) | High confidence that neither is **current law**, verified against ILGA's own bill-status pages |
| 225 ILCS 330/5 (professional land surveyor licensing framework) | Low — general framework citation, no UAS-specific guidance located |
| Executive orders / AG opinions / court decisions / general procurement statute | Low — negative research finding, not a comprehensive search |

Consult Illinois counsel for project-specific compliance determinations. Local ordinances and tribal UAS considerations are out of scope for this phase per current research instructions.*
